note: Taxpayer rights, record retention and the appointment checklist. Rights titles are from the IRS Taxpayer Bill of Rights (public domain); summaries are our own words.

items.title: The right to be informed
items.body: You have the right to know what you need to do to follow the tax laws, and to clear explanations of IRS decisions and letters.

items.title: The right to quality service
items.body: You have the right to prompt, courteous, and professional help, and to speak with a supervisor about poor service.

items.title: The right to pay no more than the correct amount of tax
items.body: You only owe the tax that is legally due, including interest and penalties, and the IRS should apply your payments properly.

items.title: The right to challenge the IRS’s position and be heard
items.body: You can object to IRS actions, provide documents, and expect the IRS to consider them promptly and fairly.

items.title: The right to appeal an IRS decision in an independent forum
items.body: Most IRS decisions can be appealed to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, and many can be taken to court.

items.title: The right to finality
items.body: You have the right to know how long the IRS has to audit a year or collect a debt, and when an audit is finished.

items.title: The right to privacy
items.body: IRS inquiries and enforcement should go no further than needed and should respect due process.

items.title: The right to confidentiality
items.body: Information you give the IRS is generally not shared unless you allow it or the law requires it.

items.title: The right to retain representation
items.body: You can choose an authorized representative to deal with the IRS for you, and you may be able to get help from a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic.

items.title: The right to a fair and just tax system
items.body: The IRS should consider facts that affect your ability to pay, and you can get help from the Taxpayer Advocate Service if problems aren’t resolved through normal channels.

items.title: 3 years
items.body: Keep records that support your return for 3 years from the date you filed (or the due date, if later).

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: 3 years from filing, or 2 years from paying
items.situation: You filed a claim for a credit or refund after filing your return
items.body: Keep records for 3 years from when you filed the original return or 2 years from when you paid the tax, whichever is later.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: 6 years
items.situation: Income you should have reported was left off, and it’s more than 25% of the gross income on the return

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: 7 years
items.situation: You claim a loss from worthless securities or a bad debt deduction

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: At least 4 years
items.body: Keep them at least 4 years after the tax is due or paid, whichever is later.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: Until 3+ years after you sell
items.situation: Records about property (a home, rental, investments, business equipment)
items.body: Keep them until the period of limitations ends for the year you sell or otherwise dispose of the property, because they show your cost and improvements.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: Indefinitely
items.situation: You didn’t file a return, or a fraudulent return was filed
items.body: There is no time limit in these cases, so keep records indefinitely.

sources.title: IRS: How long should I keep records?

items.title: About you and your family
list: Photo ID for you (and your spouse, if filing jointly)
Social Security cards or ITIN letters for everyone on the return
Birth dates for dependents
Last year’s tax returns (federal, Ohio, and local)
Any letters from the IRS, Ohio, RITA, or CCA
Your bank’s routing and account number, if you want direct deposit (bring it in person; please don’t email it)

items.title: Income
list: W-2s from every job (boxes 18–20 show local tax withheld)
1099-NEC or 1099-K for contract or gig work
Records of business income and expenses
1099-INT and 1099-DIV for interest and dividends
1099-B or brokerage statements for investment sales
1099-R for pensions, annuities, and IRA withdrawals
SSA-1099 for Social Security benefits
1099-G for unemployment or state tax refunds
Schedule K-1s from partnerships, S corporations, estates, or trusts
Rental income and expense records

items.title: Deductions and credits
list: Form 1098 for mortgage interest
Property tax statements
Receipts for charitable donations
Medical and dental expense records, if large
Child care provider’s name, address, tax ID, and amount paid
Form 1098-T for college tuition and 1098-E for student loan interest
Retirement and HSA contribution records
Form 1095-A if you had Marketplace health insurance

items.title: Taxes you already paid
list: Dates and amounts of federal estimated tax payments
Ohio and local estimated payments
Any payment made with an extension request
